name: enca
why: Guesses character encodings from byte statistics, a neat look into how text bytes reveal their language, though a mature utility.

brief.what_it_is: Enca (Extremely Naive Charset Analyser) is a command-line tool and C library that detects the character set and encoding of text files and can convert them to other encodings. It has two parts: libenca, the detection library, and enca, a command-line frontend that wraps libenca and several conversion backends. The homepage and README do not describe the output format in detail, and the scout note's claim about byte statistics is not stated in either page I fetched. The fetched pages also list the enconv executable name only through the catalogue metadata, not in the README text.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes Enca as an Extremely Naive Charset Analyser that detects encodings of text files and can also convert them. The README gives no further motivation.
brief.how_it_works: libenca performs the detection and supports a set of languages (Belarusian, Bulgarian, Croatian, Czech, Estonian, Finnish, Hungarian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Polish, Russian, Slovak, Slovene, Ukrainian, Chinese) plus some multibyte encodings regardless of language. For conversion, the enca frontend can use a built-in converter or external tools: GNU recode, UNIX98 iconv (libiconv), Perl Unicode::Map or Unicode::Map8, and cstocs. The README does not explain the detection algorithm itself.

brief.install_notes: Build from source with the standard autotools flow. Optional configure switches: --with-librecode[=DIR] / --without-librecode for GNU recode, --with-libiconv[=DIR] / --without-libiconv for iconv, and --enable-external / --disable-external for external converter programs (enabled by default). External converters (GNU recode, Unicode::Map8 or Unicode::Map, cstocs) are optional. No accounts or runtime services are needed. I did not see a Homebrew-specific note; brew caveats were empty.
brief.standout: It is a small, long-lived C tool built around per-language detection for Central and Eastern European languages, a niche where many general tools are weaker. The README's own framing is modest ('Extremely Naive'), which reads as an honest description of a statistics-driven approach rather than a neural or ML detector.
brief.status: Quiet on releases but apparently being picked up again. The homepage's most recent blog post is 'Enca 1.19' dated Sept. 5, 2016, and the download section lists 1.19 as current. The README has copyright lines through 2025-2026 for a new contributor and points to a Project-OSS-Revival GitHub organisation, which suggests a revival effort. I did not see a last-commit date, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The README says Enca should compile on any POSIX.1 system with an ISO C compiler, but it needs several standard headers and a working string.h, and some noncompliant systems are mentioned without detail. Several README URLs disagree: the homepage points to github.com/nijel/enca, while the README's 'Web resources' and 'Bugs' sections point to github.com/Project-OSS-Revival/enca. The README also says the library API is only relatively stable ('it will either change only marginally, or very drastically'). Licence is GPL version 2. The README's language list does not include all languages one might expect, and it covers only the listed languages plus multibyte encodings.
